rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results - the authors collected their own 2018 time-series of UAV RGB imagery (five dates), EMI soil ECa surveys (four dates), in-situ soil sensors, soil samples and combine-harvester yield on a ~20 ha commercial soybean field in Humphrey, Arkansas, and report correlations (Tables 2-3, Figs 4-10).
rows.notes: The study uses UAV imagery to map plant spatial abundance, vigor (GCC) and height and identifies 'anomalous areas' of persistently low plant development, which it attributes to soil clay content (high ECa), short-term saturation under furrow irrigation and a late-season soil-moisture decline in the west section. It does not detect pests, diseases or nutrient deficiencies, and it does not test any intervention or its effect on production; it only reports correlations between UAV products and yield. Supports at most the precondition (detection of soil-driven growth anomalies) of the claimed detection-then-intervention effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results - own UAV, EMI, soil-sensor, soil-sample and yield data from one soybean field in Arkansas, 2018 season, with correlation analyses reported in Tables 2-3.
rows.notes: No sprayers, IoT devices, fertilizer or pesticide applications appear in the study. An SVM classifier is applied to UAV RGB imagery to separate plants from soil and to flag low-abundance/low-vigor zones, but these zones are related to soil texture and moisture, not to pest infestation, and no targeted input application or resulting change in chemical use or crop health is tested. The study only supplies a precondition (image-based identification of affected zones).

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results - own field dataset (UAV time-series, EMI surveys, soil sensors, soil samples, combine yield) from a single soybean field in Arkansas, 2018.
rows.notes: The study contains no pest detection, no pesticide application and no pest-control outcome. The UAV-based anomaly mapping identifies areas of poor plant development driven by clay content, furrow-irrigation saturation and drying in the west section; the paper explicitly interprets these as soil/water effects. At most an upstream precondition (zone identification from imagery) for the claimed pest-control effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-field, single-season observational study integrating UAV RGB products with EMI soil ECa and yield; it reports no pest, disease or nutrient diagnostics and no management interventions, so none of the three claims is directly supported.
